interviewQuestions.question: Explain what an operating system does, in one sentence?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd frame it as: an operating system shares finite hardware among competing programs, and hides that hardware's messy details behind clean, uniform interfaces. Those are its two jobs — resource manager and abstraction layer — and every OS feature traces back to one of them.

Concretely: when two processes both want the CPU, the scheduler (resource management) decides who runs and for how long. When a program calls `write()` to save a file, it never touches disk sectors directly — the filesystem and driver stack (abstraction) translate that into the actual hardware protocol.

I'd close by naming why interviewers ask this: it's easy to memorize "the OS manages the computer," but naming both jobs specifically is what shows you actually understand the model rather than reciting a textbook line.

**Testing:** whether you have a precise mental model of an OS instead of a vague one-liner.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: The one-sentence definition

interviewQuestions.question: What's the difference between an operating system and a kernel?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd start with the containment relationship: the kernel is the privileged core of the OS — scheduler, memory manager, device drivers, filesystem implementation — that runs with direct hardware access. The operating system is a larger bundle: the kernel plus system programs like the shell, standard libraries, compilers, and utilities that most users interact with day to day.

The cleanest real-world example is the Linux-vs-GNU/Linux naming debate: Linux itself is only a kernel. What most people run day-to-day is that kernel combined with a GNU-derived userland — shell, coreutils, compiler toolchain — which is why some call the whole thing "GNU/Linux" precisely to make this distinction.

Why it matters in practice: when you compare "Ubuntu vs Android," you're usually comparing OS-level choices (init system, package manager, userland) even though both share the same Linux kernel underneath.

**Testing:** whether you can draw the containment boundary precisely instead of using "OS" and "kernel" interchangeably.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: OS vs kernel

interviewQuestions.question: What's the practical difference between multiprogramming, multitasking, and timesharing?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd untangle these by their original motivations rather than treating them as synonyms. Multiprogramming's goal is simply keeping the CPU busy — load several jobs into memory so when one blocks on I/O, another can run; there's no promise of fast switching, and early batch systems used it purely for throughput.

Multitasking adds speed: switching between jobs fast enough that execution looks concurrent even on a single core, which is what makes an interactive OS feel responsive rather than batch-like.

Timesharing is multitasking's interactive use case — many users at terminals, each slicing CPU time so finely they individually feel like they have the whole machine. I'd give the concrete example: a 1970s Unix system serving 50 terminal users off one CPU was timesharing; a modern laptop juggling your browser, editor, and music player is multitasking; a mainframe batch system from the 1960s running jobs back-to-back overnight was multiprogramming without ever being either of the other two.

**Testing:** whether you know these terms have distinct historical meanings instead of using them interchangeably.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Terminology precision

interviewQuestions.question: Is a hypervisor an operating system? Where do containers fit into this picture?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd answer yes, functionally — a hypervisor does the same two jobs an OS does, just one layer up: it resource-manages physical CPU, RAM, and disk among multiple guest operating systems, and it abstracts that hardware as virtual hardware each guest OS believes is real and exclusive to it.

Containers invert the model rather than repeating it. There's no guest kernel and no virtual hardware — a container is a set of Linux namespaces (controlling what a process can see: its own PID tree, filesystem view, network stack) and cgroups (controlling what it can use: CPU shares, memory limits), all enforced by one shared host kernel. That's why containers start in milliseconds and VMs take seconds to minutes — a container isn't booting an OS, it's just being handed a restricted view of one that's already running.

The interview trap I'd flag explicitly: calling a container "a lightweight VM" is a common but technically wrong shortcut — it has no hypervisor and no guest kernel at all.

**Testing:** whether you can place virtualization and containerization on the same resource-manager/abstraction-layer framework instead of treating them as unrelated buzzwords.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Hypervisors vs containers
